referenceContext.quote: CornCorn Market Under Harvest Pressure as EU Imports Surge and Ukraine Flows StutterCMBCMB News EditorialEditorial DeskOctober 28, 2026Corn futures stay weak as US harvest and strong Argentina supply weigh on prices, while EU imports rise and Ukrainian exports via Black Sea remain uncertain.Corn markets remain under downward pressure, with futures on both sides of the Atlantic near recent lows as the U.S. harvest advances and Argentina’s crop outlook improves. Physical corn in key EU cash markets has stabilized after a sharp pullback, but underlying sentiment stays bearish given ample global supply and still-fragile Ukrainian export logistics. Amid this weakness, EU import demand for corn is robust and well ahead of last year, helped by reduced barley exports and competitive offers from the U.S., Brazil and, earlier in the season, Ukraine. However, fresh Ukrainian volumes into the EU have slowed markedly in the latest week, underlining ongoing risks around Black Sea and Danube logistics. For European feed users, current prices offer attractive coverage opportunities, while producers face a challenging margin environment. Prices Euronext corn (Nov 2026) last traded at 283.25 EUR/t, with the benchmark Mar 2027 contract at 263.25 EUR/t and slightly lower along the nearby curve, reflecting persistent pressure but a modest inverse versus more distant months. The curve turns noticeably lower by late 2027–2028, with Nov 2027 at 226.50 EUR/t and Nov 2028 at 207.50 EUR/t, signalling expectations of comfortable medium-term supply. At the CBOT, front-month Dec 2026 corn stands around 449.50 USc/bu, only marginally above the previous close after hitting its lowest settlement since 2 July amid harvest pressure and a firmer U.S. dollar. The U.S. market remains capped by large supplies and the prospect of higher ending stocks, as also highlighted by recent global balance assessments. In the cash market, German feed corn EXW Drentwede is quoted at 0.27 EUR/kg (feed grade, 14% moisture max), down from 0.275 EUR/kg on 26 October, extending the gradual decline seen since mid-October. In Chicago, Dec 2026 corn lost 6.25 USc/bu on the day to close at 448.75 USc/bu, underlining the prevailing bearish tone. The downtrend on the U.S. market has continued, driven primarily by the ongoing U.S. harvest and a stronger dollar against the euro, yen and pound, which erodes export competitiveness from the U.S. side. The U.S. harvest is now well advanced, with around 60% of corn area reported harvested as of the week ending 25 October, moderately behind some recent fast years but sufficient to keep steady selling pressure on futures and basis levels. The combination of another large U.S. crop and improving export competition from South America is contributing to expectations of higher U.S. ending stocks in 2026/27. Argentina is reinforcing the global supply cushion: the USDA agricultural attaché in Buenos Aires has raised the country’s corn production forecast from 55 to 62 million tonnes, sharply improving the outlook after previous weather-related setbacks. This upgrade is a key bearish driver for international benchmarks, especially for the deferred 2027 contracts, as it signals greater export availability from the first half of 2027 onward. In Europe, fundamental signals are more nuanced. German cash corn prices recovered slightly on Tuesday after steep declines on Friday and Monday, reflecting still relatively tight local availability. Nonetheless, EU import flows remain strong, helping to cap domestic prices and balance the feed grain complex. referenceContext.quote: CornUkraine’s High-Moisture Corn: Supply Delayed, Quality at RiskCMBCMB News EditorialEditorial DeskOctober 28, 2026Low prices, high drying costs and logistics issues push Ukrainian farmers to delay corn harvest into spring 2027, reshaping export timing and quality risks.Low grain prices, high drying costs and constrained logistics are pushing a growing number of Ukrainian farmers to leave corn in the field over winter, delaying a portion of 2026/27 supply into spring 2027 while raising quality and food-safety risks. The corn market is being reshaped less by crop volume than by the timing and quality of exportable Ukrainian supplies. Producers facing moisture levels above 30% in northern and central regions are increasingly unwilling to harvest at a loss, especially as logistics bottlenecks and leftover stocks from previous seasons limit storage and export capacity. At the same time, drier southern fields have largely been harvested, creating a two-speed crop with uneven quality. The result is a near-term abundance of low-priced, high-cost-to-move corn within Ukraine, but growing uncertainty about how much of it will still meet export-grade standards by late winter. Prices Domestic and export-oriented Ukrainian corn prices remain under pressure as new-crop supply collides with limited logistics. Recent market assessments show FOB Ukraine corn around $230/mt, while CPT Black Sea indices point to flat values despite harvest progress, indicating subdued buying interest and weak export pull. Company-level indications support the picture of depressed internal prices: several farms report that the value of wet corn barely covers, or even falls short of, combined drying, handling and freight costs. This aligns with consultancy data showing EXW and CPT Ukraine corn trading at notable discounts to FOB benchmarks amid high inland logistics and drying expenses. TG Agro in the Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions plans to leave about 80% of its corn acreage unharvested over winter, while ATK expects to postpone harvesting on roughly 70% of its crop. Individual farmers such as Dmytro Solomakha are considering similar decisions on around 30% of their fields. The trigger is economics: in northern and western areas, moisture levels of 26–34% mean that mechanical harvest followed by artificial drying can be commercially unviable at today’s grain prices. Industry estimates suggest that drying costs alone may approach or exceed the farmgate value of the grain in some cases, particularly where on-farm energy prices and elevator tariffs are high. At the same time, Ukraine’s logistics system remains constrained. High transport tariffs, expensive alternative export corridors and delays shipping carryover stocks from previous harvests are tying up storage and capital. Official and industry data indicate that corn harvesting is running well behind historical pace, while early-October exports are markedly below last year. For many producers, leaving grain standing acts as a temporary “storage in the field” solution to bridge this bottleneck. Not all companies can afford such a strategy. HarvEast, for example, plans to complete harvesting before spring to avoid yield and quality losses and to protect the 2027 planting schedule. To compensate for limited conventional storage, the company is deploying polymer grain bags. Zakhidnyi Buh also targets completion between mid-November and early December, signalling that better-capitalised operators still view timely harvest as the lesser risk. In the south, ATK has already finished harvesting corn fields with average moisture around 14.7%, pointing to relatively favourable drying costs and faster marketability. By contrast, fields in Zhytomyr are showing moisture as high as 32–34%, making them prime candidates for delayed harvest. Weather has also clipped yield potential in some central regions. At Peremoha farm in Cherkasy, summer drought cut corn yields to about 4 t/ha, compared with earlier expectations of 8–10 t/ha. While this reduces local supply, it does not offset nationwide volume sufficiently to tighten the market given the broader logistics and price context. Delaying harvest allows cobs to dry naturally, cutting energy costs and easing pressure on overbooked dryers. However, it introduces significant agronomic and commercial risks. Corn left standing through winter is more exposed to stalk lodging, ear loss, pest damage and weathering, all of which can reduce harvestable volume and test weight. Fusarium infection and resulting mycotoxin contamination are particular concerns. Prolonged field exposure in damp or freeze-thaw conditions can sharply degrade grain quality. Zakhidnyi Buh has already warned that corn harvested after winter may be suitable mainly for industrial processing rather than premium feed or food channels if quality deteriorates. This implies that a noticeable share of the 2026 crop could be effectively downgraded by spring 2027, limiting the pool of export-grade material even if nominal tonnage remains high. Weather & Near-Term Outlook Seasonal forecasts for November in Ukraine point to near-normal temperatures with mixed precipitation patterns across key corn belts. Such conditions could permit gradual field drying in some regions but also raise the risk of intermittent rains and wet snow, especially in northern oblasts, which may increase lodging and disease pressure. If early winter remains relatively mild and dry, farmers delaying harvest could benefit from lower moisture content and reduced drying bills. However, any shift toward persistent wet or stormy weather would quickly tilt the balance toward higher quality losses. Given the already high share of unharvested area, weather over the coming 6–8 weeks will be critical for how much of Ukraine’s corn ends up in export channels versus domestic industrial or low-grade feed use. Market & Trading Outlook Short term (next 1–3 months): Global benchmarks are likely to stay capped by heavy nearby Ukrainian and EU supply, while Ukraine’s internal prices remain compressed by drying and freight costs. Basis variability by moisture, location and delivery term will be wide. Late winter to spring 2027: If significant volumes remain in the field, quality downgrades and mycotoxin concerns may tighten effective export supply, potentially widening spreads between top-grade Ukrainian corn and downgraded or industrial-only lots. Risk balance: Downside risk dominates for low-quality, high-moisture or logistically remote corn, whereas upside risk increases for dry, promptly deliverable parcels that meet strict feed and food specs. Strategic Pointers for Market Participants Feed buyers (EU, Mediterranean): Use current weakness to secure coverage in export-grade Ukrainian and EU origins, but insist on tight quality and mycotoxin clauses, especially for late-winter shipment windows. Ukrainian producers: Carefully model field-drying savings versus potential yield and quality losses. Where moisture is already in the mid-20s and storage is available, prioritise timely harvest to preserve export options. Traders & logistics firms: Consider differentiated pricing grids that reward low moisture and early delivery. There may be value in structuring industrial-use flows for downgraded post-winter corn if export standards cannot be met. 3-Day Directional Price Indication Ukraine (FOB Odesa, non-organic corn, EUR): Sideways to slightly softer; abundant unsold supply and costly inland logistics offset any external support. referenceContext.quote: US soybean oil demand moves up again in September as soybean oil stocks slide to 12-year low For a seventh consecutive month, implied US soybean oil consumption moved up in September, as stockpiles declined to their lowest level since 2014. October 19, 2026 By Amanda Luhavalja Agriculture Soy Soy oil Data released by the National Oilseed Processors Association (NOPA) on October 15 showed that soybean oil stocks among members were down by 12.3% on the month to 1.05 billion pounds in September, from 1.20 billion pounds in August. The latest stock figure was also down by 15.3% from 1.24 billion pounds of soybean oil in September 2025. NOPA members process about 99% of all US soybeans. In the US, soybean oil is the primary vegetable oil feedstock used in the production of biomass-based diesel and renewable diesel fuel. Demand for soybean oil started to increase earlier in the year, particularly from the biofuel sector, amid increased clarity regarding the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit and the finalization of 2026-2027 Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) biofuel blending mandates. Still, in the last month or so, biofuel sector demand for soybean oil and other feedstocks slowed, market sources said, with several biofuel production plants reportedly offline for planned and unplanned maintenance at the US Gulf Coast and in the Midwest. The latest NOPA data also showed that as US soybean oil stocks continued to decrease, soybean crush also extended lower in September, slipping to a 13-month low at 196.3 million bushels. The September crush was down by 4.4% from 205.456 million bushels in August. Trading sources attributed the sharp month-on-month decline in soybean crush to a normal seasonal slowdown in operations and a weather-related slowdown in processing across the western US Corn Belt. In the second half of September, crushers struggled to procure soybeans following heavy rains in parts of the Midwest that impacted soybean quality and caused harvest delays. Crushers in and around Iowa were the most impacted, with some running tight or out of soybeans, trading sources said. US soybean crush hit record highs earlier this year amid solid processing margins and strong domestic soybean oil demand. The crush industry has been expanding since 2021, with the build-out progressing through facility upgrades and the construction of new plants to meet increased demand for soybean oil from the US biofuel and food and feed sectors. In mid-September, CHS announced it would proceed with the construction of a proposed $770 million processing plant near Evansville, Wisconsin. The new facility will have the capacity to process 80 million bushels of soybeans each year. Completion is targeted for the fall of 2028. In its monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) released Friday October 9, USDA maintained its outlook for 2026-2027 US soybean oil consumption for biofuel production at 17.8 billion pounds. This is up by 22% from an expected 14.55 billion pounds in the 2025-2026 season. US soybean oil demand from all industry sectors was anticipated to reach 30.305 billion pounds in 2025-2026 and roughly 33.11 billion pounds in the 2026-2027 season. USDA remains bullish on US soybean oil consumption heading into 2027 following the finalization of RVOs earlier this spring that expanded feedstock demand from the biofuel sector. Under the US Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), obligated parties, which include oil refiners, must blend billions of gallons of biofuel into the US fuel mix or purchase Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) from other blenders or producers each year. The latest EMTS data showed the biomass-based diesel industry is ramping up production to meet the stronger renewable blending volumes established under Set 2. referenceContext.quote: Home Agricultural market news Soybean oil prices fall amid new US biofuel proposals 11:50, 15 October 2026 Source: Spglobal Soybean oil futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) extended their decline on October 14 amid uncertainty over US biofuel policy and increasing supplies of newly harvested soybeans. The December contract fell by 1.34% to 67.11 cents/lb during the first half of the trading session, down 4.24% from the previous session’s intraday high. On October 13, prices had climbed to 70.08 cents/lb before closing at 68.02 cents/lb, down 0.89%. The main factor weighing on the market was a new proposal announced by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on October 13. The agency proposed reallocating approximately 770 mln Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) associated with exemptions granted to small refineries from renewable fuel obligations. The total volume of exemptions for 2025 amounted to 1.76 billion RINs, compared with the previously anticipated 990 mln. The reallocation is intended to preserve renewable fuel requirements, supporting demand for feedstocks used in biofuel production, particularly soybean oil. The EPA is considering two options for implementing the proposal: distributing the additional obligations equally between 2026 and 2027 or assigning the entire volume to 2027. No final decision has been made, and the public comment period will remain open until December 4. According to market participants, full reallocation had already been largely priced in, limiting the proposal’s ability to provide sustained support for futures. Instead, uncertainty over the implementation timeline increased volatility in soybean oil prices. Additional pressure on the market is coming from the accelerating US soybean harvest. According to USDA, as of October 11, American farmers had harvested 46% of soybean acreage, compared with 25% a week earlier. However, harvesting progress remains below the five-year average of 50%. Increasing arrivals of newly harvested soybeans are accompanied by more active commercial hedging, adding downward pressure on oilseed futures. The recent price decline highlights the US soybean oil market’s sensitivity to government regulation of the biofuel sector. On October 7, December CBOT soybean oil futures had already fallen by 3.19% in a single trading session, settling at 67.68 cents/lb. Future price movements will largely depend on the EPA’s final decisions regarding the allocation of biofuel obligations between 2026 and 2027, as well as the pace of new soybean crop deliveries and demand from the processing industry. Roslin Azmy Hassan, who heads the Malaysian Palm Oil Association, expects 2026 production to match or exceed the prior full-year record of 20.28 million tons set in 2025. He tied the recent lift in supply to replanted areas maturing since June, with younger palms yielding more fruit. As he put it, "The better planting material bears more fruit compared with the material used 25 years ago." He added that after an October peak, output may taper in November and December, then run into tighter conditions in 2027 due to a lingering labor shortfall and the delayed hit from El Niño. Why prices and stocks moved Palm oil is up 18% in 2026 even as Malaysia - the world's No. 2 grower - has seen inventories climb to a record. Prices have been propelled by pricier global energy linked to conflict in the Middle East, Indonesia expanding its biodiesel mandate, and expectations that El Niño will curb production ahead. Benchmark futures touched 5,049 ringgit in mid September, the highest intraday level since December 2024. On Monday in Kuala Lumpur, prices briefly climbed 1.1% to 4,821 ringgit per ton before easing to 4,779 ringgit as of 4:15 p.m. local time. The supply surge since June has been helped by replanted, higher yielding estates coming into their stride, which has padded both output and stockpiles even as prices climbed. Palm oil remains a staple ingredient in foods and biofuels, so both energy markets and biofuel policy feed into demand. Malaysia is short roughly 18,000 harvesters, which could leave about 8.6 million tons of fresh fruit bunches on the trees and translate into around 8 billion ringgit in lost revenue, or $1.96 billion. Planters have been pulling staff from maintenance to keep harvesting going, but that quick fix disrupts essentials like fertilizer application and general upkeep. The workforce gap has been hard to close. Plantations lean heavily on foreign labor, and rebuilding headcount after pandemic border curbs has been held back by quotas and tighter controls. That labor issue could combine with the delayed effects of El Niño to hit output next year, with the weather impact expected to show up more clearly in the second half of 2027. "If you don't bring in new workers next year, then you'll see the impact on production," Roslin said. What this means for your portfolio Near term, Malaysia's bumper crop supports higher inventories alongside firm prices. Looking out, the setup shifts: costs have climbed over recent years to roughly 2,600 to 3,000 ringgit per ton, and with a planned minimum wage hike next year, plantation margins face additional pressure, which may prompt companies to pare back other expenditures. Add in the potential 2027 supply drag from a thinner workforce and a lagged El Niño, and price volatility stays on the table for palm oil and related consumer goods and biofuel plays. facts.sourceTitle: Sugar Production in Thailand Expected to Decline by 2.5 Million Tonnes

referenceContext.quote: Bangkok. The Bangkok-based office of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) has projected that sugar production in Thailand will fall by 2.5 million tonnes—from 12 million tonnes in the 2025-26 season to 9.5 million tonnes in the 2026-27 season. However, given the substantial existing carryover stocks, the overall supply and availability of sugar are expected to remain favorable despite this decline in production.It is worth noting that Thailand is the world’s second-largest sugar exporter, trailing only Brazil. The USDA office estimates that Thailand’s total sugar exports for the 2026-27 marketing season will reach 7 million tonnes, comprising 3 million tonnes of raw sugar and 4 million tonnes of refined sugar. Additionally, domestic sugar consumption is projected at 3.3 million tonnes, bringing the total anticipated sugar utilization to 10.3 million tonnes. As consumption is expected to exceed production, Thailand’s surplus sugar stocks will decrease by 800,000 tonnes; nevertheless, the stock levels will remain quite high. According to the USDA office, the sugarcane crop in Thailand has been severely impacted by the El Niño weather pattern—which has led to reduced rainfall and higher temperatures—raising concerns about a significant drop in the average sugar recovery rate.
